buffer-properties-s1.title: Adding acid to three solutions
buffer-properties-s1.text: A student adds 1.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl (1.0 × 10⁻³ mol) to 100.0 mL of each solution below and records the pH before and after. The buffer uses acetic acid (pKa = 4.74).

table.caption: pH before and after adding 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol HCl

buffer-properties-s2.title: A buffer before and after an addition
buffer-properties-s2.html: Key: HA weak acid; A⁻ conjugate base; H₃O⁺ hydronium. Spectator ions and water are not drawn.

buffer-properties-s3.title: The buffer in blood
buffer-properties-s3.text: Blood plasma is buffered mainly by carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate: H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq), with pKa = 6.1 at body temperature. Normal blood has pH 7.4 and contains about 20 times as much HCO₃⁻ as H₂CO₃.

items.q: Which claim do the data support?
options: The acetic acid / acetate mixture resists a pH change
The three solutions resist a change in pH to the same extent
NaCl solution is a buffer because it contains ions
Water resists a change in pH better than the mixture

why.correct: The mixture's pH moved by 0.09 units; water and NaCl solution each dropped by about 5.0.
options: Right: the weak acid/conjugate base pair absorbed the H₃O⁺.
The pH changes differ by a factor of about 50.
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ do not react with H₃O⁺, so NaCl solution behaves like water.
Water changed by about 5 pH units, far more than the buffer.

items.q: Which equation shows how the mixture removes the added acid?
options: H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH + H₂O
H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O + H₂O (with OH⁻ from water)
H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ → HCl + H₂O
CH₃COOH + H₂O → CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺

why.correct: The added H₃O⁺ is taken up by the base of the pair, acetate, which becomes acetic acid.
options: Right: the conjugate base consumes added acid.
There is very little OH⁻ in an acidic buffer; the acetate does the work.
Cl⁻, the conjugate base of a strong acid, does not take protons.
This is the ionization of acetic acid, which would add H₃O⁺, not remove it.

items.q: Show how the "pH after" for the mixture was calculated: find the pH after the HCl is added.

mistakes.why: Value: the changes run the wrong way. Added H₃O⁺ uses up acetate (0.010 → 0.009 mol) and makes acetic acid (0.010 → 0.011 mol).
Value: that ignores the buffer. The H₃O⁺ reacts with acetate first.

why.correct: Before: 0.0100 mol CH₃COOH and 0.0100 mol CH₃COO⁻. After H₃O⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH: 0.0110 mol acid, 0.0090 mol acetate. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × 0.0110/0.0090 = 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ M; pH = 4.65.

items.q: After the HCl is added to the buffer, predict the change in each compared with before.

variables.name: Moles of CH₃COO⁻
variables.why: Acetate reacts with the added H₃O⁺ to make acetic acid.

variables.name: Moles of CH₃COOH
variables.why: Each acetate that takes a proton becomes an acetic acid molecule.

variables.name: pH
variables.why: The ratio [CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] falls a little, so the pH falls a little.

why.correct: The buffer turns the added strong acid into weak acid, so the pH drops only slightly.

items.q: Two OH⁻ ions are added to Box 1. Which box shows the result?
options: Box 3
Box 2
Box 4
Box 1, unchanged

why.correct: OH⁻ + HA → A⁻ + H₂O: two HA become two A⁻, giving 3 HA and 7 A⁻.
options: Right: base removes HA and makes A⁻.
Box 2 is what two added H₃O⁺ ions would produce.
Box 4 shows free H₃O⁺ that has not reacted, which a buffer does not allow.
The particles change: the buffer works by reacting with what is added.

items.q: A student adds two H₃O⁺ ions to Box 1 and draws Box 4 as the result. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: The H₃O⁺ should have reacted with A⁻, giving 7 HA and 3 A⁻
The H₃O⁺ should have reacted with HA, giving 3 HA and 7 A⁻
Nothing is wrong: added ions stay free in a buffer
The H₃O⁺ should have become two OH⁻ ions

why.correct: Added H₃O⁺ reacts with A⁻ essentially to completion (H₃O⁺ + A⁻ → HA + H₂O), so it cannot sit beside 5 unreacted A⁻ ions. The correct drawing is Box 2.
options: Right: the conjugate base consumes the added acid.
H₃O⁺ is an acid; it reacts with the base of the pair, A⁻, not with HA.
If added ions stayed free, the mixture would not be a buffer.
An acid does not turn into a base; it gives its proton to A⁻.

items.q: The weak acid has pKa 4.74. What is the pH of the solution shown in Box 2?

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is inverted. [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = Ka × 7/3.

why.correct: [H₃O⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 7/3 = 4.2 × 10⁻⁵ M; pH = 4.37. The volume cancels, so particle counts can be used directly.

items.q: Box 1 is diluted with water to twice its volume. How does its pH change?
options: It stays about the same, because the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] is unchanged
It rises by about 0.30, because the concentrations are halved
It falls, because water is added
It rises to 7, because the buffer is diluted

why.correct: Both [HA] and [A⁻] are halved, so their ratio stays 1 and [H₃O⁺] = Ka × 1. The pH depends on the ratio, not on the absolute concentrations.
options: Right: dilution leaves the ratio alone.
Halving both concentrations cancels in the ratio; the pH does not shift by log 2.
Water does not add H₃O⁺ to a buffer in any amount that matters.
A diluted buffer keeps its pH until it is so dilute that water's own ions matter.

items.q: During hard exercise, lactic acid enters the blood. Which reaction keeps the pH from dropping sharply?
options: H₃O⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → H₂CO₃ + H₂O
H₂CO₃ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻ + H₂O
H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ → 2 H₂O
HCO₃⁻ + H₂O → CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺

why.correct: The added acid is taken up by the base of the pair, HCO₃⁻.
options: Right: hydrogen carbonate consumes added acid.
This is how the buffer handles added base.
At pH 7.4 blood holds well under 10⁻⁶ M OH⁻, far too little to absorb the acid.
This adds H₃O⁺; it would lower the pH further.

items.q: Taking pKa = 6.10, what is [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃] in blood at pH 7.35, the low end of the normal range?

mistakes.why: Value: that is [H₂CO₃]/[HCO₃⁻]. pH is above pKa, so the base form is in the majority.

why.correct: [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃] = 10^(pH − pKa) = 10^(7.35 − 6.10) = 10^1.25 = 17.8, which is 18 to two significant figures (two decimal places in the exponent). A little below the 20 : 1 of pH 7.40.

items.q: Based on its 20 : 1 ratio, the blood buffer is better at neutralizing which kind of addition?
options: Added acid, because there is much more HCO₃⁻ than H₂CO₃
Added base, because there is much more HCO₃⁻ than H₂CO₃
Both equally, because it is a buffer
Neither, because pH 7.4 is far from pKa

why.correct: Added acid is removed by HCO₃⁻, which is plentiful. Added base must be removed by H₂CO₃, which is scarce. This suits the body, which produces more acid than base in metabolism.
options: Right: the plentiful component handles acid.
Added base reacts with H₂CO₃, the minor component.
A buffer with unequal amounts resists one direction better than the other.
It still buffers: both components are present in large amounts.

items.q: A person hyperventilates (breathes fast), removing CO₂, which lowers [H₂CO₃] in the blood. Predict the change in each.

variables.name: [H₂CO₃]
variables.why: Breathing out CO₂ removes it, and CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ shifts left.

variables.name: Ratio [HCO₃⁻]/[H₂CO₃]
variables.why: The denominator falls, so the ratio rises.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: A larger base-to-acid ratio means a higher pH.

why.correct: Removing the acid of the buffer pair raises the ratio and the pH: this is why hyperventilating makes blood more basic.

items.q: Two buffers are made with the same weak acid: Buffer A has 0.10 M HA and 0.10 M A⁻; Buffer B has 1.0 M HA and 1.0 M A⁻. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: They have the same pH
Buffer B can absorb more added acid before its pH changes much
Buffer B has a lower pH, because it has more acid
Buffer A has a higher pH, because it is more dilute

why.correct: Same ratio, same pH. Buffer B holds ten times as much of each component, so it can take ten times as much added acid or base.
options: Right: pH depends on the ratio, which is 1 in both.
Right: more moles of A⁻ available to react with added acid.
It also has more A⁻; only the ratio matters for pH.
Dilution with the same ratio leaves the pH unchanged.

items.q: Why does a buffer contain a weak acid and its conjugate base, rather than a strong acid and its conjugate base?
options: The conjugate base of a weak acid is a strong enough base to react with added H₃O⁺
Strong acids evaporate from solution
Strong acids have no conjugate base
Weak acids make H₃O⁺ faster than strong acids

why.correct: A⁻ from a weak acid takes protons from H₃O⁺ essentially completely. Cl⁻ from HCl has a negligible Kb and leaves added H₃O⁺ free.
options: Right: the conjugate base must react with added acid.
Most strong acids are not volatile in solution; this is not the reason.
Every acid has a conjugate base; Cl⁻ is HCl's.
The speed of proton transfer is not the issue; the extent of reaction is.

items.q: A 1.00 L buffer contains 0.250 mol CH₃COOH and 0.250 mol CH₃COONa (pKa 4.74). What is the pH after 0.050 mol of NaOH is added (no volume change)?

mistakes.why: Value: added OH⁻ converts HA to A⁻, so the acid goes down (0.200 mol) and the conjugate base goes up (0.300 mol).
Value: that treats the NaOH as if no buffer were present. It reacts with the acetic acid first.

items.q: A student writes: "A buffer keeps its pH constant no matter what is added." Which correction is best?
options: A buffer limits the change; the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] still shifts a little
A buffer keeps its pH constant for added base but not for acid
A buffer works by changing its Ka to match whatever is added
A buffer keeps its pH constant until it is heated

why.correct: Each addition converts some of one component into the other, so the ratio and pH change slightly. A buffer reduces the change; it does not remove it.
options: Right: resists, does not prevent.
A buffer handles both acid and base, and neither leaves the pH exactly constant.
Ka is fixed at a given temperature.
Even without heating, additions change the pH slightly.
